Engineering Topics: Compilation, Memory, FFI, Databases, and Networking

The pages so far taught language features with programs. This page is the prose companion: how a program is compiled, how memory works, how foreign functions are called, and where databases and networking live. The chapter prints only one compiled example — the Vec pair below, which makes the 8-byte-slot layout claim concrete. Databases and networking stay prose because their code surfaces are not part of this chapter's verified snippet set, and this chapter does not print code it has not run.

How an SLA Program Is Compiled

SLA source is type- and ownership-checked by the SLA frontend, lowered to SA text, and compiled to a native executable by the SA host — the same sa sla build-exe route that built every program in this chapter. Ownership is verified twice over: once by the SLA checker, and again at the SA level by the Referee, which judges the actual instructions (the Locked_Read / Locked_Mut decisions behind the borrow examples). There is no separate interpreter and no bytecode step in the route used here. The deeper account is Ownership and Borrowing: Referee vs the Borrow Checker.

The Memory Model in One Paragraph

There is no garbage collector. Values are owned, moves transfer ownership, borrows are views whose read/write use the Referee judges, and shared state goes through Arc plus locks or through channel handoff — the shapes verified on the concurrency page. One concrete layout fact worth knowing before you size a data structure: SLA Vec elements occupy fixed 8-byte slots, so a Vec of small structs uses more memory than the packed layout a Rust programmer expects; the surface census tracks this and related gaps in Rust std × sa_std Surface Census and Gap Table.

A compiled Vec example

Both programs below were compiled and run; both print 5 35 (length, then the sum of 1, 4, 7, 10, 13). The SLA side spells the loop explicitly because the generic for-in collection protocol is still on the Phase-6 gap list.

// Rust
fn main() {
    let mut v: Vec<i64> = Vec::new();
    for i in 0..5 { v.push(i * 3 + 1); }
    let mut sum = 0;
    for x in &v { sum += *x; }
    println!("{} {}", v.len(), sum);
}
// output: 5 35
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/vec.sa"

fn main() -> i32 {
    let v: Vec<i64> = Vec::new();
    let i: i64 = 0;
    while i < 5 { v.push(i * 3 + 1); i = i + 1; }
    let sum: i64 = 0;
    let j: i64 = 0;
    while j < 5 { sum = sum + v[j]; j = j + 1; }
    println("{} {}", v.len(), sum);
    return 0;
}
// output: 5 35

FFI: the Standard Library Is the First Example

Every program in this chapter already calls foreign functions: the sa_std/... imports at the top of each file are SA-level extern declaration surfaces (.sai files), and SLA code calls through them directly — printing, formatting, tasks, channels, and locks all arrive this way. There is no binding-generator step between the declaration surface and the SLA call site. Fallible externs report errors as a Result, matched with Ok / Err exactly like the user-level Result on the error-handling page, so native and SLA-level failures share one handling style.

Databases

Database access is not part of the stock toolchain used to verify this chapter: it ships as the separate db plugin, so — by this chapter's own rule — no database code is printed here. The concepts to carry in: the plugin is an embedded store, not a database server; it has no network listener and no SQL parser; access is controlled by capability grants that are checked when a program registers its data operations, rather than by string-built queries at run time. The full treatment, including the comparison with SQLite, is the db Database Plugin section.

Networking

Networking lives one level down from the pages so far: in sa_std at the SA level, as extern surfaces, with a generated SLA thin wrapper (sla_std/wrap/net.sla, which includes TcpListener) over them. No user-level networking program is in this chapter's verified set, so — again by the chapter's rule — this page describes the shape and points onward instead of printing unverified code: the standard-library reference's networking page is the stdlib networking topic, and the census page above records how the surface compares with Rust's std::net.

Key Points of This Page

  • Compile route: SLA check → SA text → native executable via the SA host; ownership is judged by the checker and again by the Referee.
  • No garbage collector; ownership, moves, and Arc/channel coordination carry the memory model. Vec elements occupy fixed 8-byte slots.
  • FFI is the everyday case: sa_std .sai extern surfaces are called directly from SLA; fallible externs return Result.
  • Databases ship as the separate db plugin (embedded, capability-checked, no SQL) — see the db section; networking is an SA-level sa_std surface with a generated SLA wrapper — see the stdlib networking topic.
